results.message: Give me one line that sums up what you believe.

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We believe a person can fail and still be held, because the shepherd's bond with the flock is stronger than the failure. A named man is answerable for you. The road back is examined and walked in the open, not granted on request, but it is real. We baptize infants because a newborn has contracted the old death's contagion, and Cyprian's council wrote: “Even the greatest sinners, who had sinned much against God, are granted forgiveness of sins when they later believe. No one is kept from baptism and grace. How much more, then, should we shrink from keeping back an infant! Being newly born, he has not sinned, except in one way. Born in the flesh as Adam’s child, he caught the infection of the ancient death at his very first birth. For this very reason he comes the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins. What is forgiven him is not his own sins, but the sins of another.”

We argue hard and stay. One of our bishops ruled one way on the font given outside, and the other ruled oppositely a century and a half later, and neither put the other outside our table.

glosses.plain_meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, the flock is not the church in general. It is the particular people one bishop is given, in one place. He answers for them, and they can hold him to it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener often hears 'flock' as soft and a little patronizing -- pious language for churchgoers, gentle on the pastor's side, passive on theirs, and 'bishop' as a regional administrator several removes from ordinary life. We do not mean either. The flock is a charge that can be lost, and its failure is reckoned to the one who holds it. Our people are not passive: they elect, they demand, and they can force a bishop's hand. And the bishop is not remote -- he is the man who preached to you himself and knows which of you did not come.
false_friend: a soft, sentimental way of describing churchgoers, with a passive congregation and a gently benevolent pastor
a bishop understood as a remote regional administrator rather than the man who preaches to these people himself and knows who did not come

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, grace is the insistence that no effort of ours is enough on its own. Any good a person does was given to them before they did it.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, grace means this: no one's own effort is ever enough. Whatever good a person does was given to them first.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear grace as a warm general benevolence, or as 'grace under pressure,' or as a denominational shibboleth they may already have an opinion about, and to hear our anti-Pelagian position as harsh determinism. We mean a specific and contested claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity, argued against a named opponent over roughly a decade, with direct consequences for how a congregation is taught, how failure is handled, and what a pastor can reasonably ask of anyone.
false_friend: a warm general benevolence, or 'grace under pressure,' with no specific claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity
a denominational shibboleth in a Protestant-Catholic argument the participant may already hold an opinion about

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised (Doc_01 SS2; lpc.story.election-of-cyprian); banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258 (lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian)

Our claim that this is a cross-phase pattern rests on both bishops' own conduct of the office, not on matching word-counts in each phase (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes, Lexicon_Deployment_Index.md SS6).

The entire evidentiary base for this term is one voice (Augustine) within one evidence stream (the anti-Pelagian corpus), flagged at generation rather than discovered afterwards (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). No Pelagian first-person answer survives in our own record. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, kept on its own axis, independent of this historical-fact rating. The contest type is Relationship to present-day traditions, secondarily Meaning. It runs over how the historical position stands to the way living traditions use the word now, including later appropriations and the Catholic-Protestant disagreements that ran through them, and over the modern reassessment of whether the position Augustine argued against is the one Pelagius held. The entry does not present the anti-Pelagian position as the settled meaning of the word across Christian history, and it does not characterize Pelagius.

elements.surface: “Even the greatest sinners, who had sinned much against God, are granted forgiveness of sins when they later believe. No one is kept from baptism and grace. How much more, then, should we shrink from keeping back an infant! Being newly born, he has not sinned, except in one way. Born in the flesh as Adam’s child, he caught the infection of the ancient death at his very first birth. For this very reason he comes the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins. What is forgiven him is not his own sins, but the sins of another.”
